implementation_notes: The abstract-factory hierarchy collapses into a table: std::function<std::unique_ptr<Product>()> is the builder type, an unordered_map keyed by string (or by an enum or type_index) is the kit, and one register/create pair is the whole interface. std::function stores the callable by value, so a lambda may capture the dependencies (pool, logger, configuration) that the registering module chose, while callers still see only a key and the Product abstraction; returning std::unique_ptr keeps ownership explicit. Keep the map in a function-local static (Meyers singleton) so its initialization is lazy and cannot lose a static-initialization-order race, and prefer this variant when load order should be deterministic. The classic per-family factory classes remain justified only when creation is fixed at compile time and must be checked by the compiler.
pitfalls: The table must be a function-local static: a namespace-scope map consumed by another object's constructor is the classic static-initialization-order fiasco.
std::function copies its target, so a heavy captured object is copied into the table and a lambda capturing by reference dangles as soon as the registering scope ends.

Registrations in translation units that nothing else references can be discarded by the linker (dead-stripping) once self-registration is used; link with --whole-archive or assert the registry contents at startup.

variants.name: Self-registering Registrar<T> (registration before main)
variants.idiom_name: template<class T> struct Registrar holding an inline static data member
variants.implementation_notes: Each concrete type registers itself: a Registrar<T> whose constructor calls the factory's add() is instantiated once per type as an inline static data member (C++17), so the table is filled during static initialization and no central list of types exists anywhere. Choose this variant when the types live in separate translation units or arrive with plugins and nobody should have to edit the factory; note that it moves the failure modes rather than removing them - order is unspecified, and unreferenced units may be dropped by the linker. Prefer the explicit-registration variant when load order must be deterministic or the registry must be testable without link tricks.
pitfalls: Registration order across translation units is unspecified: the table must tolerate any order and no registrar may depend on another type already being present.
If nothing references a translation unit, its registrar may be optimized away; plugin-style builds need whole-archive linking or a startup assertion that the registry is non-empty.
A registrar constructor must not touch other namespace-scope objects that may not be initialized yet - the factory's own table has to be a function-local static.
